title: Cookies Policy — Hamlet
text: Cookies Policy — Hamlet hamlet . Sign in Cookies Policy Effective Date: April 2026 Last Updated: 17 October 2026 What are cookies? Cookies are small text files placed on your device to store information about your visit. They help websites remember preferences and provide a better browsing experience. How we use cookies We use cookies for essential site functionality (session management), analytics (to improve the Site) and optional features such as remembering preference settings. Third-party services (for example Google Analytics and Stripe) may set cookies when you use those features. Types of cookies we use Essential cookies — required for core functionality (sign-in, security). Performance & analytics — used to measure and improve how the Site is used. Functional — remember user preferences and settings. Third-party — cookies set by external providers for payments, analytics or widgets. Managing cookies You can control or delete cookies through your browser settings. If you disable cookies, some parts of the Site may not function correctly. To manage consent on this Site use the cookie bar presented in the footer. Changes We may update this Cookies Policy from time to time. We will post changes on this page with an updated effective date. Contact For questions about cookies or privacy, contact us at support@mail.hamlet-ai.co.uk . title: Account and Data Deletion — Hamlet
text: Account and Data Deletion — Hamlet hamlet . Sign in Account and Data Deletion Effective date: October 2026 Your choice You can delete your Impact in Business Recruitment account yourself. The option is on the Account Settings page. Deletion is permanent and cannot be undone. After it completes, that account can no longer be used to sign in. How to delete your account Follow these steps in the app: Open the site and sign in at Sign in . You must be signed in to the account you want to delete. Open Account Settings . From a signed-in page, use the members menu and choose Account Settings (the gear item). You can also go directly to /settings.html . On Account Settings, review the account details (name, email, user ID and last login) so you are sure this is the right account. Select the red Delete Your Account button under the account details card. Confirm in the dialog that says: “Are you sure you want to permanently delete your account? This cannot be undone.” Choose OK to continue, or Cancel to keep the account. If the app asks you to sign in again, complete the Google sign-in prompt. This is required when the current session is not recent enough to delete the account. After you reauthenticate, deletion continues automatically. When deletion succeeds, the app shows “Your account has been deleted.” and returns you to the sign-in page. If you are not signed in, the button is not available. Sign in first, then return to Account Settings. If deletion fails, the app shows an error message. Sign in again and repeat the steps, or contact us using the address below. What this deletes The Delete Your Account button deletes the signed-in authentication account, including the sign-in identity tied to that user ID. You will be signed out and will not be able to access members-only areas with that account. Profile and other records stored separately from the authentication account (for example a public profile document linked to your user ID) are not always removed by the button alone. To ask us to delete remaining personal data associated with the account, email support@mail.hamlet-ai.co.uk from the address on the account, include your user ID if you still have it, and state that you want associated data deleted. What we may keep We may retain limited information where we have to, including payment and invoice records, records needed to resolve a dispute, and information we must keep to meet a legal, tax or accounting obligation. Retained records are kept only for as long as that purpose requires and are not used to restore a deleted account. See our Privacy Policy for how we retain personal data. If you cannot use the button If you cannot sign in, or the delete button does not complete, email support@mail.hamlet-ai.co.uk with the subject “Account deletion request”. Include the email address on the account and, if you know it, the user ID shown on Account Settings. We will verify the request and delete the account and associated personal data we hold, subject to the retention limits above. Changes We may update this page if the deletion steps change. We will post changes here with an updated effective date. Contact For questions about account or data deletion, contact us at support@mail.hamlet-ai.co.uk . Search releases All GitHub releases ↗ Loading published installer archive… Install and verify Download the installer and the matching SHA256SUMS.txt file from the same release. Review Windows security or publisher prompts before proceeding. Do not bypass a warning if you cannot establish that the file is authentic. i Security and update guidance SHA-256 verification checks file integrity; it does not independently prove publisher identity. title: IBR Fees and Listings Access Policy — Hamlet
text: IBR Fees and Listings Access Policy — Hamlet hamlet . Sign in IBR Fees and Listings Access Policy Effective Date: April 2026 Last Updated: 18 October 2026 1. Commission on residential and commercial listings Impact in Business Recruitment Group Limited (“IBR”) does not charge commission in relation to residential or commercial property listings. No listing commission, transaction success fee or percentage of a sale, purchase, lease or letting is payable to IBR merely because a property is submitted, published, viewed, introduced through or discussed using Hamlet. A software licence fee does apply for use of the Hamlet platform. This is a charge for software/platform access, not a property commission. Applicable subscription options and prices are set out on the Pricing page . 2. Information you choose to publish Brokers should only submit details that they are content to have made publicly available through the listings gallery and associated member-facing property resources. This includes contact information such as email addresses and/or telephone numbers . Do not submit confidential, commercially sensitive, personal, or third-party information unless you have the right and appropriate authority to disclose it. 3. Responsibility for listing information Users are liable for the information they post in the listings gallery. You should ensure that property descriptions, availability information, contact details, URLs and other particulars are accurate, lawful and suitable for publication. By submitting a listing, you accept responsibility for the content associated with that listing and for ensuring that you have the necessary authority to provide it. 4. Fraud, misuse and authentication Fraudulent, misleading, abusive or otherwise improper use of the property listings service will be dealt with swiftly in accordance with our applicable policy on user authentication and account security. Access to the listings service is tied to authenticated user accounts. We may suspend or remove access where information appears fraudulent, materially misleading, unauthorised, or otherwise inconsistent with our site rules and security requirements. 5. Practical guidance for brokers Only publish information you wish to be made publicly available. Check property and contact details before submitting a listing. Do not use the listings gallery to publish confidential information. Report suspected fraud or materially misleading information promptly to support@mail.hamlet-ai.co.uk . 6. Contact Questions about this policy, the introductory commission arrangement or a listing should be directed to support@mail.hamlet-ai.co.uk . 7. Scope of service and no agency appointment Unless separately agreed in a written instruction signed by the relevant parties, access to the platform is a listing and broker-network facility only. It does not, by itself, appoint Impact in Business Recruitment Group Limited (“IBR”) as an estate agent, introduce a client on exclusive terms, or authorise IBR to negotiate, agree, or bind any party to a sale, letting, lease, or other property transaction. Any agency appointment must be documented separately, with its scope, duration, authority and remuneration clearly agreed in writing. 8. Software licence fees and other charges The software licence or subscription fee is charged for access to the Hamlet platform in accordance with the applicable plan and pricing published on the Pricing page . The fee is separate from property listings and is not a commission on a residential or commercial property, a sale, a purchase, a lease or a letting. Premium membership is an annual plan; other available subscription options are described on the Pricing page. IBR does not charge commission in relation to residential or commercial listings. No separate transaction fee, success fee, referral payment, marketing expense or other charge should be inferred from a listing or from this policy. If IBR offers a genuinely separate paid service or a third-party cost may arise, its scope, amount or calculation, payment trigger and any applicable VAT must be disclosed in writing and agreed before the service begins. 9. Introductions and non-circumvention Use of Hamlet, or an introduction arising from a residential or commercial listing, does not create a commission entitlement, success fee or non-circumvention obligation in favour of IBR. IBR does not charge commission in relation to residential or commercial listings. Any genuinely separate arrangement between other parties is independent of IBR's software licence fee and must be documented and agreed by those parties themselves. Members must not represent that IBR is entitled to a transaction fee or commission unless a separate, lawful written agreement expressly establishes that entitlement. 10. Conflicts of interest and referral benefits Members must disclose any material conflict of interest relevant to a proposed property transaction and must not misrepresent whom they represent. Where IBR or a member may receive a referral fee, commission, gift or other benefit connected with a recommendation or introduction, the relevant interest should be disclosed clearly and in writing to the affected party before they rely on that recommendation. 11. Due diligence and property particulars Members should undertake proportionate checks before marketing or relying on property information, including their authority to act, the identity and authority of the instructing party, material title or occupational information available to them, and any restrictions on marketing or disclosure. Do not describe a property as available, verified, authorised or exclusively instructed unless you have reasonable grounds to do so. Platform publication is not a survey, valuation, title investigation, legal review, planning assessment, or verification of a property's ownership, condition, income, or suitability. Interested parties should obtain their own legal, tax, valuation, building and other professional advice as appropriate. 12. Anti-fraud, sanctions and source of funds Members must not use the service to facilitate fraud, bribery, money laundering, terrorist financing, sanctions evasion, or any unlawful transaction. Where applicable to their role, members remain responsible for complying with their own legal and regulatory obligations, including identity checks, customer due diligence, record keeping and suspicious-activity reporting. IBR may request reasonable supporting information, restrict a listing, or suspend access while a credible concern is reviewed. Any action will be subject to applicable law and the relevant contractual terms. 13. Confidentiality, privacy and data protection Do not upload confidential information or personal data unless you have a lawful basis and authority to share it for the stated purpose. Share only the information reasonably necessary, keep it accurate, and take appropriate steps to protect it from unauthorised access or disclosure. Personal data handled through the platform is also subject to the applicable Privacy Policy and data protection law. Members remain responsible for their own handling of information they obtain from other members and prospective counterparties. 14. Intellectual property and permitted use Members must have permission to use photographs, floor plans, descriptions, logos, documents and other material they submit. By uploading material, a member confirms that doing so does not knowingly infringe another person's rights and grants IBR the limited permission reasonably required to host, display and operate the listing service. Members must not scrape, bulk-copy, resell, republish or otherwise misuse listing data or platform content, except where authorised by IBR or permitted by law. 15. Listing moderation, suspension and removal IBR may review, decline, amend for presentation, hide or remove a listing where it reasonably considers that the listing is inaccurate, unauthorised, unlawful, misleading, unsafe, reported as fraudulent, or inconsistent with the platform's terms or this policy. Where practicable, IBR may seek clarification before taking action, but urgent protective action may be taken where appropriate. Members should promptly update or withdraw listings that are no longer available or whose material particulars have changed. 16. No guarantee and limitation of responsibility The platform is provided to help members share and discover information. IBR does not guarantee that a listing is accurate, that a transaction will proceed, that a counterparty is suitable, or that a property will meet a user's requirements. Members must make their own enquiries and decisions. Nothing in this policy excludes or limits liability where doing so would be unlawful, including liability that cannot legally be excluded. Any other allocation of liability must be read subject to the applicable terms of service and any separately signed agreement. 17. Complaints and dispute handling Raise policy, listing or fee concerns promptly and in writing with support@mail.hamlet-ai.co.uk , providing the listing reference, relevant dates and supporting details. IBR will review the information available and may request further evidence from the parties involved. Members should seek to resolve commercial disagreements professionally and preserve relevant records. This process does not prevent a party from exercising any legal rights or remedies available to them. 18. Changes to this policy IBR may update this policy to reflect changes to the service, commercial practice or applicable law. The revised version will be published on this page with an updated revision date. Changes to any separately agreed fee or agency appointment will be governed by the terms of that agreement and applicable law; publication of a revised policy does not, by itself, vary a separate contract. 19. Applicable law and interpretation This policy should be read alongside the site's Terms of Service, Privacy Policy and Cookie Policy. It does not replace a signed agency agreement, property contract or professional advice. Applicable law and jurisdiction are determined by the relevant contractual terms and mandatory legal rules; nothing in this section is intended to override those rules. References to legal or professional standards are intended as practical guidance and do not imply that IBR is regulated by, or is a member of, a professional body unless that status is separately and accurately stated. title: EnerPHit | Retrofit certification and energy standards
text: EnerPHit | Retrofit certification and energy standards hamlet . by IBR Search Back to Hamlet Retrofit · Building performance · Real estate EnerPHit: rigorous energy performance for existing buildings EnerPHit is the Passive House Institute’s certification standard for energy-efficient retrofits of existing buildings. It recognises that upgrading an established building can be constrained by its structure, geometry, heritage features, occupants and construction history—yet can still achieve a substantial improvement in energy demand, comfort and building quality. Why it matters: For office landlords, logistics operators, housing providers and asset managers, an evidence-led retrofit can reduce operational energy demand while preserving useful building stock. EnerPHit provides a defined route to independent assessment rather than relying on unverified efficiency claims. Background and purpose The Passive House Institute (PHI), established by Wolfgang Feist in Darmstadt in 1996, developed the EnerPHit standard to address the practical challenges of improving existing buildings. Whereas the Passivhaus standard is frequently associated with new construction, EnerPHit applies Passive House building-physics principles to deep refurbishment. Its premise is to improve the thermal envelope, airtightness, ventilation and building services as far as reasonably achievable, with performance verified through modelling, construction evidence and testing. It is not a generic label for any renovation that reduces energy bills. Certification can be pursued for suitable residential and non-residential buildings. The current PHI criteria, building use and climate determine the applicable thresholds and verification requirements. Core principles of a high-performance retrofit Successful refurbishment starts with understanding the existing fabric, its defects and its operating conditions. Measures should be coordinated so that improvements in one area do not create moisture, ventilation or overheating problems elsewhere. 01 Assess the existing building Survey construction details, defects, thermal bridges, damp, air leakage, ventilation and plant before specifying works. Use measured information where practicable. 02 Upgrade the thermal envelope Improve walls, roofs, floors and glazing with attention to junctions, heritage constraints, fire safety and moisture risk. 03 Improve airtightness Develop a continuous airtight layer and test it. Controlled ventilation becomes particularly important as uncontrolled leakage is reduced. 04 Provide effective ventilation Design fresh-air supply and extract for actual occupancy and use. Heat recovery can reduce heating demand where suitable. 05 Manage summer comfort Consider shading, glazing, internal gains, ventilation and future climate conditions so that winter improvements do not increase overheating risk. 06 Coordinate services and controls Right-size heating and cooling systems after demand reduction; commission equipment, controls and ventilation for the intended use. Retrofit sequencing: In occupied buildings, works may be staged around leases, business continuity or household needs. PHI provides a recognised pathway for step-by-step projects through a documented retrofit plan, subject to its specific requirements. EnerPHit certification and verification EnerPHit certification is an independent assessment against PHI criteria for existing buildings. Depending on the applicable criteria, a project may follow an energy-demand method or a building-component method . The former evaluates specified energy-performance targets; the latter focuses on qualifying building components and associated requirements when demand targets are not the appropriate route. Neither route removes the need for project documentation and quality assurance. Confirm eligibility and scope. Engage a qualified certifier early; establish the building boundary, use, climate, constraints and current criteria version. Survey and model. Record existing conditions and model proposed improvements using the Passive House Planning Package (PHPP) and the applicable EnerPHit method. Prepare the retrofit strategy. Coordinate insulation, windows, thermal bridges, airtightness, ventilation, heating and cooling. Address moisture and overheating risks. Document construction. Retain drawings, product specifications, photographs of concealed details and evidence of changes made on site. Test and commission. Undertake required airtightness tests and building-services checks, including ventilation commissioning as applicable. Submit for independent review. The certifier checks the completed model and evidence, requests corrections where necessary and determines whether the project meets the standard. Verification is not the same as a predicted bill saving. Certification assesses compliance with defined technical criteria; actual energy consumption also depends on weather, occupant behaviour, equipment, operating hours and maintenance. Check the certificate, scope, date and certifying body rather than relying solely on marketing language. Retrofitting the built environment The best measures differ between asset classes. The following examples show how a performance-led approach may translate into property decisions. Offices Commercial workplaces Envelope and glazing improvements can reduce heating and cooling loads, while ventilation and controls must reflect meeting-room density, equipment gains, changing occupancy and tenant fit-outs. Industrial & logistics Warehouses and distribution Conditioned areas, loading doors, dock operations and high-volume spaces create distinct challenges. Refrigeration and process loads may dominate consumption and require separate assessment. Residential Houses and apartment blocks Coordinated insulation, ventilation and window upgrades can improve comfort and reduce heating demand. Resident disruption, damp risks, tenure and common services shape delivery. Public estate Schools and civic buildings Seasonal schedules, high occupancy and procurement constraints require careful phasing, ventilation design and commissioning. Hospitality Hotels and mixed-use assets Continuous operation, hot-water demand and varying space uses mean that zoning and system design are central to a credible retrofit. Heritage Constrained and historic buildings Protected façades and traditional fabric may limit external insulation or window replacement. Specialist conservation and moisture-risk expertise are essential. Other energy-efficiency standards and assessment frameworks EnerPHit is one of several ways to evaluate buildings. The frameworks below answer different questions: some certify a design or retrofit, others rate measured energy use, benchmark emissions or assess wider sustainability. They are not interchangeable certifications . Passivhaus PHI’s performance-based standard, commonly applied to new buildings, emphasises very low energy demand, comfort and verified design and construction quality. Read Hamlet’s Passivhaus guide . BREEAM A broader sustainability assessment methodology covering categories such as energy, health, materials and management. An overall BREEAM rating is not equivalent to EnerPHit energy certification. LEED A widely used green-building rating system that assesses multiple sustainability dimensions. Its energy credits and whole-building rating should be interpreted within the relevant scheme and version. NABERS and NABERS UK Operational-performance rating approaches based on measured energy use and relevant adjustments. NABERS UK focuses on office energy performance, with scope and rating rules defined by its programme. Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs) Regulatory energy ratings used in the UK and other jurisdictions under differing national methods. EPCs are not proof of EnerPHit certification and may differ from actual metered performance. ISO 50001 An international standard for organisational energy-management systems and continuous improvement. It certifies management processes rather than a particular building’s thermal-envelope performance. Selection principle: Choose the framework that fits the decision. A landlord may need regulatory compliance evidence, a measured operational rating and a fabric-performance certification for different purposes. Confirm the jurisdiction, scheme version, assessor credentials and scope before comparing assets. Implications for owners, investors and occupiers Deep retrofits can reduce energy demand and improve comfort, but their business case depends on capital expenditure, operational disruption, remaining asset life, local regulations and occupier needs. Due diligence: review baseline condition, modelled performance, certification evidence, test results and metered energy data separately. Whole-life carbon: assess embodied emissions from new materials alongside operational energy and carbon savings; replacement is not always preferable to refurbishment. Letting and operations: consider lease responsibilities, tenant equipment, metering boundaries and post-occupancy commissioning. Risk management: plan for moisture, fire safety, overheating, indoor air quality, maintenance access and future adaptation. Claims and valuation: avoid assuming that any certification guarantees rent premiums, higher valuations or specific savings. Official guidance and further reading Passive House Institute — primary source for EnerPHit building criteria, certification guidance and PHPP. Passivhaus Trust — UK-focused technical guidance, training and project resources. BREEAM — sustainability assessment methodology. LEED — green-building rating system. NABERS — measured operational building ratings. ISO 50001 — energy-management systems standard. This page is an educational overview, not a substitute for the latest certification criteria, building regulations or project-specific engineering advice. © 2026 Impact in Business Recruitment Group Limited · hamlet

title: Passivhaus | Energy performance in the built environment
text: Passivhaus | Energy performance in the built environment hamlet . by IBR Search Back to Hamlet Building performance · Real estate Passivhaus: a fabric-first standard for better buildings Passivhaus is a rigorous, performance-based building standard designed to deliver high levels of thermal comfort and indoor air quality with very low energy demand. It applies to more than houses: the same whole-building approach can inform the design and delivery of offices, education buildings and other commercial or public property. Why it matters: Passivhaus connects building design to measurable performance. For property owners, occupiers, developers and investors, certification can provide independently checked evidence that a building was planned and delivered against defined energy and quality criteria. Origins and development The Passivhaus concept emerged from research and collaboration in the late 1980s between German building physicist Wolfgang Feist and Swedish researcher Bo Adamson. Their work explored how a building could maintain comfortable indoor conditions while needing very little conventional space heating. A pioneering group of terraced homes was built in Darmstadt-Kranichstein, Germany, around 1990–91. Their monitored performance helped demonstrate that very low heating demand could be achieved in occupied buildings, rather than existing only as a theoretical design ambition. In 1996, Wolfgang Feist founded the independent Passive House Institute (PHI) in Darmstadt. The Institute developed the technical criteria, planning methods and quality-assurance approach that helped the standard spread internationally. Passivhaus is now used in residential and non-residential projects across a wide range of climates and building types. The premise: reduce demand before supplying energy Passivhaus follows a whole-building, fabric-first approach. Instead of relying mainly on large heating or cooling systems to compensate for heat loss, air leakage or overheating, the design reduces those loads at source and then provides controlled ventilation and appropriately sized building services. 01 High-performance insulation A well-insulated thermal envelope slows heat transfer through roofs, walls, floors and other exposed elements, helping internal conditions remain stable. 02 Continuous airtightness Careful detailing and construction limit uncontrolled air leakage. Airtightness reduces avoidable energy loss and helps ventilation operate as intended. 03 Thermal-bridge reduction Junctions and connections are designed to minimise local heat loss and cold spots, improving energy performance and reducing condensation risk. 04 Efficient windows and solar control High-performance glazing, suitable orientation and shading balance useful daylight and solar gains against unwanted heat loss and summer overheating. 05 Ventilation with heat recovery Mechanical ventilation supplies fresh air and removes stale air. Heat recovery can retain much of the warmth from extracted air without mixing it with incoming fresh air. 06 Modelling and quality assurance Energy modelling, detailed design, construction checks and testing are used together so that intended performance is supported by evidence, not just specification. Important distinction: Passivhaus is a performance standard, not a prescribed architectural style or a single construction system. Design solutions differ by climate, use, occupancy, operating hours and building form. The applicable criteria and modelling assumptions must suit the actual project. Applications across real estate The principles can be applied to a broad range of building types. Non-residential buildings need particular attention to their use patterns, ventilation loads, internal gains, opening hours and process requirements. Commercial Offices and workplaces Stable temperatures, filtered fresh air and reduced heating and cooling demand can support occupant comfort and help manage operational energy costs. Meeting rooms, dense occupancy, IT equipment and long working hours must be modelled realistically. Industrial & logistics Warehouses and logistics facilities Thermal-envelope quality and controlled air leakage can reduce energy demand in staff areas, offices and suitable conditioned warehouse space. High-volume spaces, frequent loading-bay openings, refrigeration and process loads require careful project-specific analysis. Residential Homes and apartment buildings Low space-heating demand, fresh air and comfortable internal surface temperatures can benefit houses and multi-unit residential developments. Design must also account for occupant behaviour, hot-water demand and summer comfort. Public & education Schools and community buildings Ventilation, high occupancy and varied schedules make good planning important. A performance-led approach can support indoor comfort while reducing energy required to condition occupied spaces. Hospitality & leisure Hotels and leisure buildings Bedrooms, shared areas and other spaces have different operating profiles. Modelling and commissioning need to reflect occupancy, hot water, humidity and any specialist ventilation requirements. Mixed use Complex and multi-use properties Where different activities share a building, zoning and energy modelling should reflect their separate schedules and loads. The standard's application should be confirmed with a qualified project team and certifier. What certification means Passivhaus certification is a voluntary, evidence-based quality-assurance process. It is intended to verify that a project meets the relevant published criteria; it is not simply a label for a building with good insulation or a low-energy design claim. Set the brief and applicable criteria. Confirm the building use, climate, boundaries of the assessment and the appropriate version of the Passive House Institute's building criteria. Model the proposed building. Use the Passive House Planning Package (PHPP) or the applicable approved method to assess energy demand and relevant performance indicators using project-specific assumptions. Develop and document the design. Record the thermal envelope, windows, junctions, ventilation strategy, systems and component data needed to substantiate the model. Manage construction quality. Resolve design details, verify critical materials and workmanship, and complete required testing, including airtightness testing and ventilation checks where applicable. Submit evidence for independent review. A qualified certifier reviews calculations, drawings, product information, test results and construction documentation against the relevant criteria. Address findings and complete certification. Any gaps must be resolved before certification can be granted. Keep the certificate and supporting records with the property's technical and asset-management documentation. Exact performance limits, evidence requirements and procedures depend on the applicable criteria version and building type. Always consult the current official criteria and engage an experienced Passivhaus designer or certifier early in the project. Relevance to commercial property owners and investors For owners, developers, occupiers and asset managers, Passivhaus can provide a disciplined framework for considering building performance over the life of an asset. Operational energy: reducing demand can lower exposure to energy-price volatility, although actual bills depend on occupancy, tariffs, controls and operational practice. Occupant experience: thermal comfort, fresh air and attention to overheating can support a better indoor environment. Asset evidence: certification and its supporting documentation can help due diligence teams assess stated design and construction performance. Design and delivery discipline: modelling and verification bring energy targets into the design, procurement and construction process. Carbon strategy: reducing energy demand can contribute to operational emissions goals, while whole-life carbon, electricity sources, refrigerants and other impacts still need separate assessment. Certification does not guarantee a particular rent, valuation, occupancy rate or financial return. Outcomes depend on location, market conditions, construction and maintenance costs, tenant requirements and how the building is operated. For logistics and other specialist property, assess process energy separately from the building's regulated or modelled energy demand. Further reading and official guidance Use primary technical sources when specifying a project or assessing a certification claim. Passive House Institute — Institute and history : background on the independent research institute and its work. Passive House Institute — Building certification and criteria : official building criteria and certification information. Passivhaus Trust — What is Passivhaus? : UK-focused overview of principles, evidence and implementation. Passipedia : technical knowledge base on the Passive House concept and building performance. © 2026 Impact in Business Recruitment Group Limited · hamlet

title: Sector Coverage | Hamlet
text: Sector Coverage | Hamlet hamlet . Sign In Back to Home Media Brief Service Sector Coverage The media brief service is focused on communications concerning the financing of three defined areas: energy, infrastructure and commercial real estate. Within commercial real estate, particular emphasis is placed on value-add investment strategies where active capital deployment, repositioning, operational improvement or development can enhance asset performance and investment value. 01 The Financing of Energy Coverage extends to financing activity associated with the energy economy, including the funding of energy assets, projects, transactions and investment programmes. The scope is intended to capture financing developments across conventional and emerging energy markets where the principal subject is the provision, structure or deployment of capital. Relevant announcements may include power purchase agreements (PPAs) , including long-term contractual arrangements underpinning the financing and revenue profile of energy projects, as well as financing-led transactions involving the acquisition of energy assets or businesses. Coverage also extends to announcements concerning downsizing and strategic restructuring where changes to the scale or composition of an energy business have material financing, investment or capital-allocation implications, together with leadership appointments involving senior executives responsible for capital, investment, financing or strategic direction. Coverage: energy finance, PPAs, acquisitions, strategic downsizing and leadership appointments. 02 The Financing of Infrastructure Coverage applies to financing connected with infrastructure assets and programmes, including transactions in which long-term capital is required to develop, maintain, refinance or expand essential infrastructure. The emphasis is on the financing dimension of infrastructure announcements rather than on general infrastructure commentary without a material funding or investment component. Coverage also includes leadership appointments across sustainable infrastructure, real assets and ESG functions, particularly where senior appointments relate to investment, capital deployment, asset management, sustainability strategy, responsible investment or the long-term stewardship of infrastructure portfolios. Such announcements may include appointments to investment, portfolio, sustainability, ESG and real-assets leadership positions where the individual has responsibility for shaping financing, investment policy, asset performance or sustainable infrastructure strategy. Coverage: infrastructure finance, infrastructure investment and appointments across sustainable infrastructure, real assets and ESG. 03 The Financing of Commercial Real Estate Coverage includes financing matters relating to commercial real estate assets, portfolios and transactions, with particular emphasis on value-add investment strategies where capital is used to reposition, develop, improve or actively enhance the performance of commercial property. Specific areas of interest include luxury hotels, storage facilities, logistics assets and last-mile capital investments . These strategies are especially relevant where disciplined investment, redevelopment, operational enhancement or targeted capital expenditure is central to creating additional asset value. The relevant focus is the financing dimension of these investments, including debt, equity and other forms of institutional or transactional capital supporting acquisition, development, refurbishment, refinancing or expansion. Coverage: value-add commercial real estate finance and investment. Scope of service. Sector coverage describes the subject matter for which the media brief service is intended. It is not a statement of investment advice, underwriting, financial intermediation or professional suitability, and the service may decline briefs that fall outside the defined sector remit.
